Mr. Speaker, the motion put forward today by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) seeks to establish a special committee of this House, conveniently ignoring the fact that we have been, you might say, in a special committee debating the budget for the last several days and well could be for further days to come. The motion seeks to establish a special committee to determine whether the federal tax structure is inhibiting economic growth in Canada and promoting the export of employment opportunities to the United States.
I suggest the motion implies that Canadian economic growth is losing out to the Americans. In the first place that assertion has not been proven by the hon. member himself in his rather inconclusive suggestions and remarks put forward, or by any other speaker from the opposition benches. Secondly, there is the assumption in his motion that tax structures in the United States are considerably more advantageous and

therefore more attractive to both business and workers in the United States of America.
The hon. member tried to tell us in his introductory remarks that medical care and hospitalization, which costs a good deal in this country to provide and which no group of Canadians and no political party wants to be without, are available in the U.S. at considerably less cost.
His motion conveniently ignores the basic differences in the nature and the scale of the economies of both countries. He seeks to compare only the tax structure. He does not look at the fact, for example, the state of New York in the eastern U.S.A. was roughly equivalent a few years ago to the total Canadian population. For another example, one can cite the state of California on the west side of the United States where there is a population tenfold that of Canada. My hon. friend seeks to compare the two countries without any recognition of this basic fact.
I suggest the motion is a typical Conservative effort, the kind of thing we have heard from members opposite for many months now to downgrade the country and promote the concept they have worked at practically since the beginning of this session on January 23. At that time the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) wound up his first question in the House on January 23 like this:
I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. This is the first day of parliament in 1978, a year which looks like it will become known as the year the country closes down.
That has been the kind of rhetoric and negativism that we have heard for a considerable period of time from members opposite.
My hon. friend is concerned about the civil servants. He has made his speeches here and elsewhere concerning the civil servants of this country. We could go into that topic-if he chooses! I suggest we could leave that one until later. I could perhaps comment on that suggestion of his later on as well.
I want to suggest that the budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) of April 10 is and represents the kind of responsible change in tax structure that this country needs. Perhaps we need more of it, that is true, but hon. members opposite have so far not advanced any additional measures of their own, other than an income tax reduction to further add to the existing deficit about which they continue to express some considerable concern.
The budget of April 10 contained a number of specific measures to deal with economic growth, to promote greater short-term growth, at the same time looking at some of the long-term problems as well. I suggest to my hon. friends opposite that rather than embark on a study of United States tax structures they would be best advised to adopt these measures put forward by the Minister of Finance in his budget just as quickly as possible, and put forward some of their own specific suggestions as well while they are at it. Instead, they have chosen to delay the budget and prolong the debate.
In the course of that they have chosen a new route for the Conservatives. It is not surprising really because any route is a
May 23, 1978

good route for them. They have chosen to side with the PQ government of Quebec, judging by press and media reports. They have chosen not to debate the budget and the changes put forward, but rather to engage in the phony issue at this point in time of provincial rights. This is an issue which was manufactured and put together by the Levesque government in Quebec whose sole purpose in existing as a government is to dismember the country, and we have our friends opposite siding with that government.
One can forgive provincial political parties in Quebec for standing up with the Levesque government on the question of provincial rights. It has long been part of the Canadian political tradition to blast Ottawa, to blast the federal government at almost the drop of a hat, and to oppose federal initiatives, many of which, to varying degrees, could be said to intrude or infringe in some manner on provincial fields of responsibility. That certainly is not new. The Tory opposition fell into that trap. They condemn separatism in one speech in one part of the country, and then slide in others to make Parizeau and Levesque look more or less like Canadian heroes in this tax debate. I make this point to indicate the insincerity of the motion today to come to grips with the federal tax structure.
The April 10 budget of the Minister of Finance contained a move to reduce the provincial sales tax all across the country. It was a good move, one that deserves the support of all parties in this House. That move obtained the support of nine provinces in a joint effort to come to grips with economic problems in this country. I say again that the minister deserves the full support of the House for a very timely initiative on his part. Incidentally, that move was recommended by many economists and economic advisers of a wide variety of political stripes.
I suggest to hon. members opposite that Canadians want more action of the kind contained in the Minister of Finance's budget. Western Canadians in particular prefer action to the kind of rhetoric we have heard today from the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie).
Canadians from one coast to another are not interested in any more of the kind of grandstanding we are hearing today, that we have heard outside the House and in previous debates in the House from the official opposition. Putting forward a suggestion to establish a parliamentary committee to study American tax policy is another red herring to propagate the supposed tax advantages of the United States.

First, there is the provision to increase the tax write-off for research and development, a special allowance to permit a

deducting from taxable income of 50 per cent of the costs of increases in research and development activity. That will benefit not only the small implement manufacturers and other farm oriented types of manufacturing activity going on in western Canada, but other industrial activity there as well.
The cost of machinery, equipment and other facilities for enhanced capital recovery systems becomes eligible to earn a depletion allowance of $1 for every $2 spent, an increase from the previous $1 for every $3. That move is designed to encourage oil and gas exploration in Canada, Saskatchewan and Alberta primarily.
Another move is the increased limit on the deduction on the depletion earned on certain expenditures on non-conventional oil projects, such as the heavy oil and tar sands projects. It is increased to 50 per cent of total profit. That incentive is designed to bring about development of those programs and large bodies of primarily undeveloped sources of energy in western Canada.
Fourth, the tax-free rollover provisions apply to incorporated family farms. That goes along with the provision which has been there for some time for the unincorporated family farm. Fifth, plants established to upgrade heavy oil will be deemed to be manufacturing and processing facilities. Once again, it will give those plants a better tax advantage and tax breaks.
The final point of particular interest in western Canada is that an additional capital cost allowance will be provided on depreciable railway system assets acquired by railways before 1983. This comes at a time when the government is putting up $175 million this year, with the promise of more money to come, to improve and upgrade not only the rail network but the running stock and other stock, as well as spending associated with rebuilding and upgrading the rail network which is so vital not only to agriculture but to other industries in western Canada. I say again that the April 10 budget certainly has been designed for western Canada. It is one that should be adopted and moved forward.
I want to take a few moments to deal with the question of capital gains tax and the provision to allow the tax-free rollover provision to be extended from the individually owned farm to the incorporated family farm. Someone said earlier today that there are probably more of those farms set up in western Canada than anywhere else.
That move has been endorsed by practically all members of all parties in the House. It will be welcomed by all members. It has certainly been promoted and pushed for by the Liberal party in western Canada, particularly in Saskatchewan and by many provincial constituency associations. I know it has also been sought by farm organizations, members opposite, and others.
It is another modification of the capital gains provisions which came into effect in 1971 at the time of the abolition of estate taxes and a number of other major changes to the income tax structure.

While I congratulate the minister and his cabinet colleagues for this particular change, I would like to see them go further in terms of modifying the capital gains tax structure. For example, to continue the 1971 valuation for land and other business assets such as buildings and facilities is not realistic in terms of the level of inflation we have had since 1971.
Over the past several years, most tax rates such as income tax and others have been indexed. Indeed, most government spending programs have been indexed. I think specifically of old age pensions, family allowances and veterans pensions. I should say that I concur in the fact that we should continue to index veterans pensions and old age pensions. I am not so sure about family allowances and some of the other programs.
If we are going to pursue indexing and adopting that principle, we should do something about the fact that farm land values across this country, in the western provinces in particular, have increased dramatically since 1971, particularly as the result of inflation. Not all of the increase is due to inflation. The temporary $5 wheat and the strong market demand were certainly a factor in pushing up land values. The depreciation of the dollar is a major factor in that upward change in land values.
The Canadian tax structure in so far as it relates to capital gains should be changed so that the taxpayer is not paying for illusory inflationary gains. Farmers and small businesses in particular will welcome the moves announced in this debate this afternoon by the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott) which will facilitate the operating of their businesses, be it farming or some other business.
I think there should be further relaxation of the provision with respect to the capital gains tax. I acknowledge the fact that last year amendments were introduced and passed allowing people who sold their land or businesses to incur no capital gains tax when the funds realized from the sale were reinvested in a similar business or purchase. That was a good move and one which will go a considerable distance, but I believe it could be extended still further.
Perhaps the idea of a once in a lifetime exemption from capital gains tax is one which we might look at. If a farmer wishes to sell his farm and take up another business, possibly within his own local community, I think he should be permitted to do so. If the tax is not remitted he should be given several years, anyway, in which to make payment. The proposal in the report of the Bryce commission that we should get out of the capital gains tax entirely might be worth considering, at least for a period, so as to stimulate entrepreneurship. I know the report did not go into much detail with regard to the inequalities such a move would create but I believe this whole complex subject of the capital gains tax and the effect it may be having on entrepreneurship and investment should be examined more closely.
I am sure that setting up a parliamentary committee as suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre is not the place to begin. A committee is not the best forum in

which to consider complex matters involving the tax structure. It is true there are a few accountants on both sides of the House but basically we are not in a position as members to inquire into specific details of tax law and suggest changes in such a complex piece of legislation as the Income Tax Act. This should not, of course, prevent our putting forward concepts and proposals embodying the changes we would like to see.
In conclusion may I say that it is long past the time when members of the official opposition should begin to turn their attention to restoring confidence in the country and promoting Canada for what it is, one of the great world democracies and an example of how people from different backgrounds and with different histories can live and work together. I submit that economic growth has been inhibited to a much greater degree by the attitude of members opposite, and others like them, than by any tax structure or bureaucratic system. I am not too optimistic that this will happen but I should like to hope that, as a result of this debate, members opposite will change their tune, become more optimistic about opportunities which still exist in Canada and demonstrate their pride in their country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTION COMMITTEE STUDY FEDERAL TAX STRUCTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is fortunate that the luck of the draw allows me to follow the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac). It is evident from the attention the House gave him that we recognize the soundness of his thinking. It was one of the rare occasions I have witnessed in the last few years upon which a member on the government side has come out with a positive and constructive suggestion.
He had to spoil his speech, of course, as any supporter of the government is obliged to do, by praising the budget of April 10. Automatic support of this kind is one of the reasons the Liberal party is disappearing in Western Canada. Young Liberal MLAs in Saskatchewan leave their party, an old, traditional party in the province which for a long time dominated the political history of Saskatchewan, giving as their reason the fact that the party supported whatever the federal Liberal party was doing in Ottawa in spite of the fact that what the federal Liberal party has done to this country in the last ten years has probably made them the champions when it comes to taking a strong country with so much potential and putting the brakes on all the forces which enable it to go ahead.
I prefer to deal with the more positive aspects of the hon. member's speech. He spoke about the case for changes in the capital gains tax. He referred sympathetically to the proposal in the Bryce report. Mr. Speaker, this is the first occasion on which I have heard a member of the Liberal party say a good word about that royal commission. We on this side have been telling the government for a long time-and I have been in a good position to do so since I myself voted in favour of the capital gains tax-that this question should be reviewed as a matter of necessity. It is a brake on our growth at the present time.
May 23, 1978

If the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley is sincere, that is why he should support the motion now before the House. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) wants us now to work on economic matters, get away from the fooling around we have been doing in the House for the last ten years and take this opportunity of a year's delay before the election to do some sound work such as we have not done for ten years. I think the hon. member would agree that since parliament is doing nothing about this suggestion of changing the capital gains tax as a result of the apparent opposition of the government, it would be wise for him to show his sincerity as a backbencher by voting for this motion. Let parliament have a chance to look at the tax legislation, get evidence from people who know something about it and then recommend ways in which we believe it could be improved.
The hon. member suggested that we in the opposition have not been coming forward with constructive proposals. All 1 can say is that he has not been reading Hansard very carefully. Idea after idea has been put forward from this side of the House to make our country stronger and better. I propose to talk about one of them today.
Last fall, when the mini-budget was brought forward, I knew the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) was in trouble. He is a well liked, ambitious, hard working young member who was suddenly pushed into the job of Minister of Finance knowing full well that every minister going back to the days of Walter Harris 30 years ago had failed in this job. It was my hope, since he appreciates the value of common sense, that he would have realized that the biggest load on the back of our nation, one which retarded our growth more than anything else and prevented the achievement of our national objectives, is the taxation system developed in the last 40 years. Ever since the war it has been clear that this restrictive tax system has been the heaviest load on all classes of people, rich and poor, in this country.
In my day I have seen young men get lucky breaks. When the oil boom first started in Alberta in 1947 and some people made a few dollars, they realized that because of our tax system they would have to take their money they had earned in the early stages when small companies were able to operate to the United States, form an American company with that money and then come back into Canada to invest it under American tax law. That was not because they were disloyal to this country. It was because, as the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) pointed out, there was no choice. If you want to go into business, you have to be able to survive. The House has avoided studying this tax system of ours ever since I have been here. On more than one occasion I have criticized heavily the people in the Department of Finance who have systematically followed a mythology of taxation which does not stand up to quantitative analysis.
I am going to give an example of what I am going to propose as a positive suggestion. I would like at least to see a select committee talk about the concept of potential budgeting. I
Taxation
spoke about this in the mini budget debate. The minister was very interested; he came over to me to talk to me about it. He said he liked that kind of idea. Later the parliamentary secretary asked me if I would put it into writing, so I wrote a positive, constructive letter to the Minister of Finance. I have a copy of it with me here. I suggested how this could be done and gave more details than I had given in my speech. I finally received a letter from the minister stating, in effect, that the idea was very sound but that it created a new principle, a new precedent. The minister said that I was asking the government to give individuals in Canada the same equity and fairness in the tax system which business gets, and he said the government could not do that because it would erode the tax base. It is not a matter of just reducing the amount of taxes owing to the government; it is a matter of the growth of the country.
For example, a French-Canadian farmer spent $85,000 over a 20-year period to develop a new technique for making every part of an implement go to the same depth in the ground. His name was Jerome Bechard. He happened to live in my constituency. The tax system would not allow him to take one cent of deduction off his farm income for the sum of close to $85,000 spent in developing a new technique for better cultivation, which would have meant many hundreds of millions of dollars each year for the farmers of the west and to any farmer who had the chance of using this big machinery in any part of the United States or Canada.
Last year an American entrepreneur took up this particular invention, which was patented and put into production, and now this French-Canadian farmer is allowed to take all his receipts for the last 20 years and deduct them from the income he makes from the small royalty he gets from the utilization of this invention of his. Thank God he waited and lived long enough to be able to find an opportunity under the tax law to deduct the huge expenses he put into developing his technology.
Another example of potential budgeting can be seen in the fact that we have to convert our country quickly from the utilization of energy from non-renewable resources. The state of the art is such that there are only a dozen or so of these technologies which come close to the economies which are necessary to make them viable. In my speech last November I put forward to the Minister of Finance, in the hope that I could help him, the suggestion that since these things were not presently being made in Canada, it would cost his budgeting nothing to say that, if any person goes ahead and tries these things out on an experimental basis, that individual should be allowed the same exemptions under the tax law that the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley mentioned: that if any person does research, he should be allowed to write the expense off his income.
The research I am talking about is not the fundamental research. That is already done. Our National Research Council has developed an upright windmill in the wind tunnel here in Ottawa. It has been written about all over the world, but no single company mass produces this windmill for sale to the public even with an 80 per cent write-off for research work. It

has to be the individual who takes it on. If civil servant scientists can make it work, I am sure that two thirds of our farmers can make it work. It runs soundly. If you put an induction motor on the bottom of it, you can pump this power into the power grids and sell your excess power to the power grids; and when the wind is not blowing, you can draw your power back from the power grids. It has been done for years in Wisconsin.
Last October the province of Saskatchewan announced its willingness to do it, but we still do not have that windmill's introduction because of the tax law. I think it is a fairly reasonable idea. It is just as reasonable as the change in the capital gains tax which many hon. members on this side have mentioned and which now has the support of the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley. It is news when a backbencher of the government supports a royal commission.
All the pundits say that no one dares to support the latest royal commission report because it is pro-business. One of the mythologies of Canadian politics is that to be "with it" you must be anti-business. That has been the curse of both the United States and Canada for the last 30 years. Most people assume a "rip-off' attitude toward business. God knows that business needs to be kicked around, but we cannot get along without it. I suggest that there is a good case to be made, considering all the ideas which have been put forward in this House. We are not getting publicity for them because it is not news to make a constructive suggestion, but let us get our suggestions into a select committee, and just maybe, in its desperation of having to face the people, the government might consider some tax changes.
Our tax system has held this country back. We have had double taxation on corporate income for all the years I have been around here, and long before that. A royal commission now recommends that we stop that double taxation. The Carter royal commission recommended it in 1969 and 1970, but no action was taken. A royal commission recommends it in 1978, and, judging by the sounds we hear from the government benches, we know what will happen to that recommendation.
The government does not want to be caught going into an election ending double taxation on business. Double taxation occurs when a corporation is taxed at the rate of 45 per cent to 50 per cent and then the fellow who has invested and who owns the corporation is also taxed. If one royal commission recommended in 1970 that we get rid of double taxation and now another royal commission recommends it, the same thing will happen as happened in the case of the last four royal commissions on transportation. The government gets busy immediately and hides the whole report on transportation. We have before us now the Hall Commission report. The government does everything to delay it, hoping to get by the election. That is what the budget was for. The deduction of sales tax for six months was designed to get the government by the election, but there is not to be an election. When the six months is up, their tail will be in the fire and the fat will really flow.

I suggest that if the Prime Minister is honest and wants parliament to go to work, then let us set up this select committee. 1 am sure that among the laymen and the few accountants on this side and among the few accountants on the government side there can be found some who could put forward some proposals, because certainly the Department of Finance ran out of ideas 30 years ago after the white paper in 1946.
As for the remarks of the hon. member for Waterloo-Cam-bridge (Mr. Saltsman), let me say that it is clear that here is a man preaching for the call. He wants to join Crowfoot on the government benches. The crow from Waterloo-Cambridge hopes that the Prime Minister will hear the call of the wild and answer his appeal.

When I heard the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge devote his whole attack to the simple idea of establishing a select committee to examine the tax law and say it was unpatriotic, that we should stay in Canada with the high taxes, and that they support the Liberal government because of their high taxes and because they are a good government, I knew that that man was preaching for the call and has been preaching for the call for a long time. He must be very jealous of the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) for having made it across the way. But what a price he had to pay! Now he has to come along and attack the poor old Conservatives.
We have not been in power since 1963 because the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has steadily led his party in support of the government. He helped defeat the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) in 1963. He helped to keep in power the minority government under Pearson, and he helped to keep in power the minority government as well as the full majority under the present Prime Minister. Is that party doing its duty of pointing out the weaknesses in the government so that we get a better government? No, sir; their main financial spokesman attacked the official opposition. I am just warning him. David Lewis destroyed the NDP in 1974. He went up and down this country attacking the Conservatives because he said their 90 days of price and wage controls would ruin the country. He frightened the labouring man in the cities into voting Liberal, and the NDP disappeared out of our cities.
Now we have another member of the NDP wanting to repeat what David Lewis did. You cannot frighten people all the time. When I was a kid, the first time I was on a farm I noticed horses coming up to the water trough. If you jumped out of the pump house and yelled "boo", they all ran. After a while, the horses stopped paying attention to it and they came to the water trough in spite of the shouting and yelling. I want to remind the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge that his



May 23, 1978

job here is to take each subject as it comes up and look at arguments for or against it. All he did was to attack the Conservatives and make charges that are as silly as the charges made by the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac). We have the right to stand for a certain federal system with the right of the province to tax without being attacked by the government in Ottawa. He stands up and says we support the PQ. How believable is that type of remark?
If the government wants to show that it will make parliament work next year, then let us set up this committee and see what we can do. Let us end this silly political science type of yelling at each other which we heard in one or two disgraceful speeches today. This is a good opportunity for serious minded members of the government to show their Prime Minister that they would like this parliament to work. Maybe we can produce some ideas that will improve this tax system. I repeat again and again that our tax system is not perfect. Our tax system must be competitive with the tax system in every other country, and it is not competitive with other countries at present. It is time to compare our tax system with that of our main opponent in business, namely the United States. Let us see if we cannot produce one that will compete, that will allow capital to flow into this country and allow Canadians as individuals to own this country instead of the large U.S. companies, the way it is now.

speechtext:
That is correct. The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge indicated that we are not talking about a brain drain when we talk about the talent which is going from Canada to the United States. He indicated that it is a "banal-

May 23, 1978
Taxation
ity drain" rather than a brain drain. A few minutes after that, I learned that he is one of the people who has an investment in a hotel in Florida. I suppose he ought to recognize banality when he sees it. He should be careful about using such terms in the House. Apparently he has a limited view of human nature.
I represent a business community in my riding which has worked hard to keep its end of the economy going. Yet in a 12-month period 66 businesses went out of operation. I asked the local chamber of commerce in Surrey to do a count of those businesses which had gone out of business, gone bankrupt, closed their resources, tightened them up, moved to another province or moved to the United States. For one reason or another, 66 companies representing 2,500 jobs went out of business in a 12-month period.
Let us assume some were mismanaged and that some may have been undercapitalized, but surely not all 66. We have to look for some other reasons. The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge said it was a "banality drain" if they go to the United States, but maybe it is a survival drain. Maybe these people want to keep their lives, their bodies, their souls together.
I know a young lady just out of university with a talent for designing clothes. She is specializing in designing tennis wear for ladies. She is very creative and loves this business. She started operation in Surrey but has found it very difficult, not because she does not have the expertise or the creativity, but because of tax, regulations and other strangleholds by the government. Out of curiosity she went to the United States and there found the freedom she wanted to expand her business. This is a brain drain rather than a move by some tired businessman who wants to get rich quickly. This is a young person who is creative and has imagination. She wants the freedom of spirit to work with her talents, but she finds the atmosphere in Canada is just too stifling.
The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge referred to the number of doctors moving to the United States, and assumed that all doctors who move there to practise medicine are doing so exclusively in order to earn more money. I suggest these are creative people, and naturally they want to earn as much as possible, as does everyone else. But that is not the only reason they are moving. As a matter of fact, a doctor acquaintance of mine who is now practising in Calgary plans to move to Texas. He is not planning to move so he can earn more money but rather because the atmosphere and the incentive in the United States for his profession are so much better.
The Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott) made some grand announcements today regarding the freedom the small business community will experience as a result of his changes in policy. He wanted us all to join in singing "Hail the Conquering Hero" because he had brought in some new measures. The Minister of Finance suggests that is what we should be doing right now. Of course, I am sure he will lead us in that singing. This is much like thanking someone who stops

hitting you on the head. This government has instituted a lot of policies that have been oppressive and a blow to businessmen. The minister now says the government is going to take away those oppressive regulations and that we should thank him for doing so. I do not know that we are in a mood for that.
I talked to one of the local businessmen in Surrey this evening about this motion. He gave me the following information regarding differences in taxation policy between Canada and the United States. He said that in Canada there is a small business deduction at the low rate of tax on up to $150,000 a year, cumulative to $750,000. That rate is 25 per cent, but it is assessed on all associated companies. If you go to the United States you will find the same kind of tax, but the tax there is on each $200,000 in a year at the rate of 25 per cent up to $50,000. That seems to be more, but when you realize that it is on up to $200,000 for each company, and the tax is not associated, you will find the tax burden is considerably less in the United States than in Canada, and there is no cumulative clause in that tax policy.
In this country we find that for manufacturers there is a 5 per cent tax credit on capital equipment. This is helpful. It can accrue to $5,000 and represents a deduction from tax payable. In the United States the tax credit is 10 per cent or 12 per cent, plus depreciation, and they are considering increasing it to 17 per cent. Perhaps some will think that is not an incentive for businesses to move from Canada to the United States. Certainly it is not responsible for a brain drain but rather has caused a survival drain. Business people like to stay alive and when they find that kind of difference in taxation policy on small businesses between Canada and the United States they move to where they can survive.
Some time ago this same businessman sent me some of his suggestions. Among other things, he said there ought to be some relief for municipalities from federal government taxation. We all know that the federal and provincial governments have first right to taxation powers and the municipalities get what is left over. For that reason the municipalities get what is left over. For that reason the municipalities use whatever source they can find, such as a tax on machinery. That may be all right when the machinery is operating at 100 per cent capacity, but when there is an economic slowdown, such as we are facing today with machinery shut down for 20 per cent, 30 per cent or 40 per cent of the time, while the tax carries on, this becomes very oppressive and only the sharpest of business people can remain in operation.
This businessman had another observation which I think is worth presenting to members of the House. It is one of those creative ideas the Minister of Finance may want to entertain. Since he likes to adopt those ideas presented by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, perhaps this is an idea he would like to accept. My business friend in Surrey suggests this:
My proposal would be to charge no duty as such at all. Instead each country would be rated by labour standards. The lower the standard, the higher the surcharge. On top of this surcharge would be a direct tax. This tax would be applicable to Canadian products as well as imported.
May 23, 1978

This type of taxing arrangement, if the details are worked out right, should be designed to give:
A.	Canadian industry the protection it needs from low-wage areas.
B.	Foreign high-wage countries a better opportunity to compete in Canada with other foreign countries.
C.	Low-wage countries a better chance to obtain a higher standard, because it will become advantageous to get classified in a higher wage category to lower their surcharge.
We are losing our markets to low-wage countries or third world countries around the world. This does not mean that the people we want to help are getting the benefit of those exports to our country. We may be buying shoes from Korea but the people who are making the money are the industrialists, the factory owners in that country; the benefits do not necessarily filter down to the working people.
What my constituent suggests is that if we set up a labour code for all countries of the world, especially applicable to third world countries, perhaps there would be some kind of incentive to those countries to upgrade their working standards, wage standards and conditions in their factories, and pass on the profits from their products to the workers. This idea represents some insight into human nature.
Everyone wants to make as much money as possible. We believe in the incentive system, but human nature is such that too often those who have money get more at the expense of those who are defenceless, particularly the masses in those third world countries. The suggestion this gentleman makes is that we provide a kind of incentive in our country through our import policies in order to encourage manufacturers, industrialists and investors in those third world countries to improve living standards for their workers which would in turn enhance their opportunity to export their products to Canada. If we do not provide that prod, it is not likely that they will do it on their own initiative.
As 1 said earlier, what we need is a proper understanding of human nature. Business people have great incentive, great inventiveness and they want to be rewarded for their work. There is nothing wrong with that but there are many people in this country who regard "profit" as a dirty word. Unconscionable profit, illicit profit, is dirty, but hard won profit is a compliment to the ingenuity, foresight and creativity of our people.
I want to compliment the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre on putting this motion before the House and bringing to our attention the very serious investment climate which is draining productivity from our country to the United States and taking manpower and personnel south of the border.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTION COMMITTEE STUDY FEDERAL TAX STRUCTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion now before us gives us an opportunity to outline the comparative performances of the Canadian and American economies as well as our fiscal structures. I welcome this opportunity and I hope that today's discussion will leave us with a better appreciation of the matter. The growing econom-
Taxation
ic closeness with the United States has been of concern to all successive ministers of finance since confederation. This is an important issue, because of the sizes and proximity of our two nations, the nature of our resources and respective attitudes, and also the free flow of capitals, goods and services across our common border.
Our two countries are interdependent. Clearly, none of my predecessors has been free to take any decision of economic policy without prior scrutiny of the impact on that economic closeness. For some people, that kind of interdependence is an unhappy or indeed untolerable situation. Such an attitude in my view is neither useful nor realistic. There is no way our two countries can be separated geographically. What we can do, is maintain the largest possible degree of freedom of action, and make the best possible use of the advantages in that huge market down south.
I would like to expand today on the comparative economic performances of our two countries during the last few years. Such differences as may be are the best pointers to our accomplishments and shortcomings in the last few years.
I will continue by dealing with certain aspects of our respective tax burdens. The economic growth curves of Canada and the United States have diverged in the last few years as almost never before. This has generally been in our favour and comes from the fact that most of the policy decisions taken in Canada were good ones. As world oil prices quadrupled in 1973 and 1974, we took advantage of our energy reserves to compensate for higher domestic oil prices. We took action to protect Canadians against inflation and the impact of a world recession. We maintained incomes and production in Canada more successully than they did in the United States. Contrary to what happened in all other industrialized countries of the world, we never had a decline in the gross national product. Real income of Canadians has continued to grow and employment has risen steadily.
Economic recovery in the U.S. was slow in coming, and it is because it was under way that for two years the rate of economic growth in that country was faster than here. That situation came as a result of the fact that the U.S. was coming out of a recession to cover lost ground. Canadian production nevertheless went up by 21 per cent last year over 1972, whereas in the United States it increased only 14 per cent over the same period. Employment in Canada over the past five years increased by 16.1 per cent, compared to 10.8 per cent in the U.S. Real disposable income per capital has risen 24.7 per cent in Canada since 1972. South of the border, it increased only by 11.8 per cent, less than half, Mr. Speaker.
On the negative side, we of course experienced a set-back in terms of costs and prices as compared to the United States. We have been concerned with this situation for several years. Our poor performance relative to the Americans is largely responsible for our present economic problems. The economic gap between our two countries was bound to have general
5658

May 23, 1978
Taxation
repercussions. It was bound, sooner or later, to lead to appreciable increases in unemployment.
As the increases in manpower unit costs were larger here than in the U.S., there were no buyers, both here and elsewhere, for a number of our products. We had to devise a way to rectify the situation and we of course implemented the prices and income control program whose main objective was to restore our competitive position. In 1975, the unit cost for labour in the manufacturing sector increased by 11.8 per cent in Canada as compared with 6 per cent in the United States, which means a margin of 5.8 per cent. That gap was gradually reduced to 5.1 per cent in 1976 and 1.8 per cent in 1977. I have repeatedly pointed out the advantage for Canadian trade and our balance of payment of the recent evolution in the rate of the Canadian dollar. Its depreciation is the answer of the market to our imbalance. It has helped restore our balance in terms of foreign trade. If we take into account the effect of the depreciation on the unit cost for labour, the latter in fact decreased last year.
As I have explained several times already, we must not bank exclusively on our floating dollar to pull us out of the whirlpool of inflation in which we were caught. To keep the gains we have registered, we must make sure there is also a decrease in the underlying rate of prices and costs increases. We have not yet restored ourselves to the strong international position that was ours in the early '70s. Unless we manage to reduce progressively the rate of increase in our costs, nothing can prevent another inflation spiral or yet another serious imbalance in our balance of payments and new depreciation of the Canadian dollar.

We have before us today a motion which implies that the tax system is behind all our problems. The motion suggests that taxes are holding down growth in Canada and forcing entrepreneurs into the United States where presumably they will get better treatment. Of course, tax levels are very important in business decisions-decisions about location of production, about expansion of production and about the balance between capital investment and employment of labour.
In Canada more than half of all revenues are collected by provincial and local governments. To a far greater degree than in the United States the second level of government shares a responsibility to ensure that the total burden of taxation is competitive on an international basis. I am glad to say that the provinces are keenly aware of this.
The communique from the first ministers' conference in February committed both levels of government to a tax policy that will establish our tax system in line with those of other trading nations. We have made a careful calculation of overall tax levels in Canada and the United States. We have made specific comparisons of personal income taxes and corporate income taxes in the two countries. It is possible, of course, to find specific states where some extraordinary tax incentives are offered to industries if they locate there. For federal and

provincial governments in this country to try to match every one of these incentives would be to sell out our tax system. We should not be in the business of creating tax havens in Canada. We should be levying a fair burden of taxes on corporations and individuals and delivering needed and effective government services to both groups in return. In fact, our comparisons of average tax burdens between Canada and the U.S.A. show that Canada is competitive.
Let me outline our main conclusions. First, over-all burdens. Despite the fact that Canadians enjoy substantially more government services than Americans, such as universal medical care, family allowances and higher old age security payments, the total level of taxation as a percentage of total output in the economy is only slightly higher in Canada. In 1977 we estimate taxes as a percentage of the g.n.p. were 32.7 per cent in Canada and 30.8 per cent in the U.S. The difference was 1.9 per cent. The difference was slightly smaller than in earlier years of the 1970s. This level of taxation ranks both Canada and the U.S. in the middle among industrialized countries.
I might note that the mix of tax revenues is quite different between Canada and the U.S. While corporation taxes are about the same in relation to total, personal income taxes and indirect taxes are relatively more important in our tax structure while social security taxes are much higher in the United States.
I should say a word about indirect taxes; that is, the federal sales tax and customs duties. I want to make it clear that the federal sales tax, which is applied at the manufacturers' level, is not charged on goods which are exported from this country. In other words, our system favours those industries which must compete internationally. This is very important. For example, if the federal sales tax were to be replaced by an increase in corporate income tax, about 15 percentage points would be added to the rate of tax on corporate profits. Clearly, the mix of Canadian taxes is favourable to the operation of business in our open economy.
As I said, the corporate income taxes take up about the same proportion of total taxes in Canada as the U.S.; the percentages are 12.3 for Canada and 11.5 for the U.S. I will come back to that in a moment.
A comparison of taxes on individuals in Canada and the United States should include social security taxes as well as income taxes. In 1977, average tax rates in Canada for these two taxes together totalled 15.8 per cent of personal income. For years these burdens have been very nearly identical on average in the countries.
I should point out that here again the structure of the system differs significantly in the two countries. Unlike Canada, the U.S. assesses tax on aggregate family income. It does not tax government transfers or pensions. It uses different rate structures for different family types, and it does not index its tax structure. The U.S. provides more itemized deductions but fewer exemptions. The Canadian system therefore tends to
May 23, 1978

be fairer since exemptions are automatically available to all taxpayers, while deductions are based on particular expenses which tend to be larger at higher income ranges. A further factor is that our dividend tax credit partly integrates personal and corporate taxes which, to some degree, eliminates double taxation on corporate income. The credit has the effect of refunding to shareholders part of the taxes already paid at the corporate level. No such mechanism exists in the U.S.
Furthermore, Canadian taxes on family income tend to be more progressive; that is, they are relatively lower at the bottom end of the income scale and higher at the top. Our system is also more favourable to families with children, and it is more favourable to families where more than one member is employed.
Let me turn to corporation income taxes. On balance, Canadian corporation income tax rates are now substantially lower than the same tax rates in the United States. In 1977, federal and provincial corporation income taxes as a percentage of corporation book profits totalled 35.2 per cent in Canada and 40.2 per cent in the U.S.A. In the important manufacturing sector, Canada's two-year write-off for machinery and equipment, together with the lower corporate tax rate of 40 per cent, gives Canadian manufacturers a much lower rate than their U.S. counterparts.
In the corporate area as well the structures of the two systems are substantially different. The Canadian rate structure is more generous with its lower general rate; that is, 46 per cent compared with 48 per cent. The Canadian federal small business deduction applies a rate of 20 per cent or 25 per cent over a large range of taxable income. A company in Canada may enjoy this rate on up to $150,000 of profits a year. In the U.S. the low rate is available on $50,000 annually only. As I mentioned, the 40 per cent manufacturing and processing rate is available in Canada.
The U.S. treatment of business losses is more generous than in Canada. In Canada all domestic intercorporate dividends are deductible while in the U.S. some dividends are not fully deductible. In the U.S. inventory valuation is made on the last-in, first-out basis. In Canada, a 3 per cent inventory valuation adjustment has been introduced. The relative generosity of these two inventory methods depends on the particular circumstances of a company.
The value of the Canadian and U.S. investment tax credits are difficult to compare because coverage differs. The rate in the U.S. is generally higher; that is, 10 per cent compared with 5 per cent, IVi per cent or 10 per cent in Canada. The Canadian credit applies to both investments in structures and in machinery and equipment. The U.S. credit does not apply to buildings but covers more industries. In the area of depreciation provisions, Canadian rates are much more favourable.
I have introduced these comparisons to make the point that in broad terms tax burdens in this country are reasonable and fully competitive with those in the U.S. In many respects, it can be argued that our tax system is fairer and provides more boost to growth and employment. But I have also pointed out that all sorts of special incentives can be found in one state or
Taxation
another, incentives that we should not try to duplicate if we are to retain the integrity of our tax system. Nor would we expect that the U.S. federal tax system would try to match every incentive offered by individual Canadian provinces.
Our job as legislators and my task as Minister of Finance, Mr. Speaker, is not to make sweetheart tax deals to entice industry to this country. Our job is to develop tax law fairly in the interest of all taxpayers. When we give up tax revenues in the interest of special deals and special privilege, we deny the use of that revenue to the benefit of other deserving Canadians. Our job is to make decisions in this chamber that will help promote a positive environment and sustain a sound economy, where business leaders will be encouraged to take the risks that are required in the market system, where worthwhile new jobs are being created, where planning and investments go forward in step with the great potential of our economy.
Above all-and I say this very seriously-we can best inspire confidence in our economy, and ensure growth and new employment, by keeping Canada united. The battle for unity is being won. When the outcome is clear to employer and investor, we will have cleared a hurdle standing in the way of our best economic performance. Certainly, we are not being held back by any lack of skills or resources in this country. And we are not being held back by the Canadian tax system.
This is a good occasion for me to speak on this because rumours are being spread across this country that our tax system is bad in relation to the American system. It was important to clear up some of that misinterpretation. We have a different tax system, but the spread is only 1.5 between the two nations. We have a much more developed social system than exists in the United States. We should be very proud of the fact that we are still in a very competitive position as far as our tax system is concerned with regard to the United States.

He says in effect that any suggestion for a review of our tax measures by the House of Commons is an attack on Canada.
What a ridiculous proposition the minister puts before us. The reason we are sitting here debating measures on allotted days and on government days is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) could not screw up his courage to call an election. As the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) says, the people did not want an election. The Prime Minister's excuse for not calling an election was that parliament had work to do.

On one of its allotted days, the opposition makes the suggestion that maybe parliament has a role in studying the tax system in Canada. It is an opportunity to review our situation today. A prima facie case has apparently been made by spokesmen in various businesses, such as construction, manufacturing and so on.
We have a situation where officials in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce are expressing serious concern about the flow of capital to real estate investment in the United States. What happens when we in the official opposition suggest that, since we are going to be sitting here for another year or so, parliament should take an active role in trying to come to terms with the taxation system of our country? It is considered by the government and its henchmen in the NDP. They support the government at will. They are going from 14 per cent to possibly 12 per cent in the next Gallup poll. That is because they keep supporting the government regardless of its policies.
We are told that this motion is some sort of an attack on Canada. They say we should be proud of having one of the highest rates of taxation, that we should be proud to sit here and listen to speeches about the beneficence of this government.
If parliament is to turn to performing a useful role and if we are to take the Prime Minister at his word, which is very difficult with his record, this motion should receive the wholehearted support of every member of this House. There should be a non-partisan, non-political look at our tax system, a review of the experience in this country with regard to the flight of capital to the United States and other countries. We should consider the extent of the problem. What has the government to fear from that kind of consideration by a committee of parliament?
There is nothing wrong with this motion. The government feels it is in a box, that it is losing the support of the country and will be turned out of office. What is its reaction to any response by this party in bringing forward a resolution that in effect allows parliament to operate? By a committee set up by this motion, parliament could consider our tax levels and mode of taxation with respect to individuals, corporations and businesses in general.
This motion gives an opportunity to the government to show it is prepared to listen, as opposed to the spectacle we saw today when there was no one here to speak on behalf of the government. That is the way they operate government. That is the way they approach matters in the House of Commons. It is a reflection of the attitude taken by this government, particularly by the Prime Minister who has absolutely no time for parliament.

The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) is renowned for making speeches from the seat of his pants. He
May 23, 1978

says the Prime Minister is here every day. I can assure the minister that it is a great honour for us to see the Prime Minister here in this chamber to answer the questions we put to him. Ele does us all a great honour. The emperor comes into parliament and gives his time to answer questions. Then at three o'clock he retires to his office to be surrounded by a phalanx of 101 members of his staff. Since I have been in parliament he has not participated in a debate on any motion or item of business before the Elouse except for the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, when he makes a contribution whose only effect is to put people all across the country to sleep.
When the Prime Minister says of members of parliament, including his own party members, that within 50 yards of Parliament Hill they are nobodies, he is revealing his attitude toward them. If I were a backbencher on the government side I would be more concerned about being a nobody while I was on Parliament Hill. The present government, more than any other in history, fears parliament. It fears debate. It fears any suggestion on our part for a constructive review of taxation and its reasons are well founded. Members opposite have placed themselves in a position where they are criticized universally for their mismanagement. They have brought a country whose potential is unsurpassed in the world to a point where there is apprehension and concern felt by citizens from coast to coast and from north to south.
My hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) is responsible for the motion which has had an immediate effect on the government. After the first round of speeches when the government whip had difficulty finding anyone to take part, in came the Minister of State for Small Business (Mr. Abbott). His face was flushed. He had no written or carefully prepared notes. The upshot was that he made a number of statements about what the government proposed to do for small business, that very important sector of society. In that act alone was an admission of guilt on the part of the government, an admission that their attitude toward the taxation of business, both individual and corporate, leaves a great deal to be desired.
There is no thought of setting out a taxation strategy with respect to business. The notion of industrial strategy is altogether foreign to them. Their only approach to these matters is the "finger in the dyke" approach. The minister talked about relieving the paper burden imposed on a limited number of businesses. Mr. Speaker, it makes no sense to come into the House and occupy time with unrelated statements which show only that the government doesn't know where it is going.
Canada is a country of unlimited potential. Nobody is standing up and saying we do not have the greatest country in the world. We do. What we have, unfortunately, is a government which leaves everything to be desired, a government in need of replacement by a new government. That is why we need an election very soon.
I want to deal in the few minutes remaining to me with some of the evidence for the existence of the problem referred
Taxation
to in the motion. People inside government who have studied this question have expressed concern about the flight of capital. I refer to a story in the Ottawa Citizen of April 20 in which Mr. Carl Wenaas, senior policy maker at the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, is quoted as saying that the federal government is concerned about increased Canadian investment in foreign real estate. According to this report he stated:
If companies are transferring funds out of the country, it is not desirable, obviously.
The article continues:
The federal government, he says, keeps close track of net direct investment abroad by Canadian firms but "we have no way of knowing if a Canadian is spending $2 million on a condominium in Florida."
Here we have a statement that records of investments outside Canada are being kept. But when we ask ministers during the question period about this flow of capital, they refuse to answer. The ministers responsible for economic planning do not give out any information on the subject, another example of the government's preoccupation with secrecy. Ministers opposite believe that only they can reach direct decisions and that parliament should have no voice in economic or financial planning. That is why my hon. friend asks that a committee be charged with studying these matters so as to determine the extent of the problem.
There are indications of its cause in a statement by Robert Dodge reported in the Dallas Times-Herald of February 19, 1978. John Meyer, vice-president for corporate relations at the Trizec Corporation of Montreal had this to say:
Canada has been taken over by a lot of planning boards and agencies. Here you have to undergo financial analysis by the government to do business. We said "Screw it" and started looking for U.S. properties.
This was a statement made by a vice-president of a very large Canadian corporation. What does Canadian Pacific Investments say about investment in Canada? Here is a story from the Montreal Gazette of May 2, 1978:
Canadian Pacific Investments of Montreal plans to continue expanding into the U.S. because business conditions are more favourable there, Willian Moodie, CPI president, told shareholders at the annual meeting yesterday.
I could go on and on quoting spokesmen for business across this country. They all indicate concern about the investment climate in Canada. Yet the government in its arrogance and its disdain for parliament refuses to accept the reasonable proposition put forward by my hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre. He proposes that we, as members representing all parts of Canada, take this opportunity to make parliament work, as the Prime Minister has asked us to do, by coming to grips with the taxation system to determine whether there are ways in which it might be improved. At present it is no secret that there is lack of confidence in the government and in the economy. Even the most ardent partisan backbencher in the Liberal party cannot deny that we are going through an economic crisis and that we face a serious prospect in the future. I am not here to gloat over that. In fact, I feel very badly about it. But when we do come forward with a reasonable proposition it is rejected out of hand by government spokesmen.

Somehow our suggestions are taken as an attack on the future of Canada. What a ridiculous proposition it is for the Minister of Finance to suggest that, because we want to study our taxation system, that is the extent of our concern about the Canadian economy. Clearly, that is one important aspect which has to be looked into by parliamentarians and by people who are involved in the governing of our country.
The Minister of State (Small Business) himself pointed out this afternoon that small business feels particular concern about bureaucratic red tape, and in response to this motion he came forward and made certain statements, attempting in small part to remove some of these items of red tape and paper work. We all know that this red tape affects business in Canada, the confidence of people in Canada and our economy. The Minister of Finance said that if we are critical of the performance of this government, somehow we are being unpatriotic. The temptation to criticize this government's mismanagement and mishandling of economic affairs is to me irresistible, and I hope I will not be considered unpatriotic if I point out the record of this minister with respect to the handling of his portfolio.
It has been my observation that during the time the present minister has been Minister of Finance there has been more criticism of our economy than under any previous minister of finance appointed by this Prime Minister. I suggest that perhaps one of the fundamental problems which underlies our economy is lack of confidence in this government.
In the last quarter of 1977, according to Bank of Canada statistics, over $180 million in direct investment was drained out of our economy, despite the improvement in trade balances. To date it has taken over $7 billion in either loans or international stand-by credits to shore up the dollar. In my estimation one of the reasons the world has so little confidence in our economy is the way this Minister of Finance has on a number of occasions dealt badly or failed to deal with serious problems facing our country.
As far as parliament is concerned the minister has been non-communicative or has given us information which has not been in accordance with the actual facts. I want to list a few of these things. The minister indicated to us in answers about the situation relating to the dollar that the dollar was not being supported by our government when in fact it was. At one stage the government was spending something over $700 million a month to support the dollar, all the while proclaiming that it was a "clean float".
Another example of the government's saying one thing and acting in another way is the retail sales tax legislation we are now considering. In trying to convince the people of Canada, we see the Prime Minister twisting and turning in his seat. He never speaks about anything, but the only time we saw him sitting in the House of Commons during a debate-and it was the subject of newspaper comments across the country-was when we watched the Minister of Finance twist and turn through the sales tax debate at second reading. speechtext:
What concerns me even more than some of these things are the answers we are getting in this parliament with respect to our economy. I am concerned about the aura of incompetence which seems to pervade this government's handling of economic matters. On March 9, the minister raised the bank rate by half a point, only to have to raise it by another half point on April 3. In the meantime, hundreds of thousands of dollars in foreign exchange reserves were flushed down the drain, together, I suggest with all respect, with the government's credibility.
This minister has put us in hock to the point where we are dependent on foreigners for our economic well-being as never before in the history of our country. For example, without the $2.1 billion the government has been forced to borrow from foreign banks, our reserves would be down to $423 million, a decline of something like 88 per cent from October of 1976.
The government is so inept that it cannot even identify the capital flows which are taking place, or it refuses to tell us. In 1977 the unidentified capital flows plus the balancing items totalled $3,176 billion. In the last quarter of 1977 money was flowing out of the country at the rate of $10 million a day, yet the government was unable or unwilling to identify publicly the reason for this haemorrhage.
I hope that in the brief time which has been available to me I have set out some of the compelling reasons why this motion should be supported by all members of the House. This motion should be supported, not in the interest of any partisan political gain by one side or the other, but in order to give an opportunity to members of parliament from both sides of the House through the medium of parliament in one of its standing committees to come to grips with and deal with the serious economic future we face. I thank hon. members for the extra time, and I thank the House for this opportunity to speak.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTION COMMITTEE STUDY FEDERAL TAX STRUCTURE
speechtext:
Very objectively, Mr. Speaker, I would like to take part in the debate on this motion proposed by the official opposition of the Canadian Parliament according to our rules of procedure which specify that a certain number of days called opposition days be set apart to allow members to introduce motions criticizing in a valid way the shortcomings of the government, so as to provide our country with an efficient administration.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to take part in the debate on the motion moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie). In this motion, the hon. member suggests that the federal tax structure inhibits the economic
May 23, 1978

growth in Canada and contributes to the brain drain towards the United States, be they financial or research brains.
Mr. Speaker, all members agree with the mover of this motion that the American rate of taxation is lower than the Canadian rate. That is recognized and accepted. But we must face facts. This rate of taxation imposed on incomes, on taxpayers, on workers is of course lower than in Canada. However, Canada's program of social services is much more extensive and equitable than in the United States. Compared to that country, our social benefits are much greater and Canadians must necessarily pay for them and be taxed on their income, in comparison with the American system.
Having said this, Mr. Speaker, it does not mean that I support the present tax system: I merely want to make a comparison from which to draw conclusions on possibilities of improving our tax system as compared with that in the United States.
Those social programs are obviously very costly and they must be paid; under our present system, the only way the government can do so is through our taxes, that is, personal income and corporate taxes. Mr. Speaker, the bill must be paid. At the present time, the bill is paid through taxes levied on income: the higher the income, the higher the tax. That system of personal income tax, setting aside that corporate taxes, bears no relation whatsoever with the tax system south of the border, in the United States.
Mr. Speaker, in the United States, in the case of the average taxpayer it is true that he seems to pay less than we do here in Canada-but after having weighed the pros and cons objectively, it will be found that, all in all, the two systems are comparable. We pay more in Canada but, on the other hand, we get more services. We have more services and so we must pay more. The Americans have fewer services, but they are satisfied because they pay less.
Some would say that it all amounts to the same thing. Why not follow the American system? In my opinion, the answer is quite simple. In Canada, those who have the highest incomes pay most services, which seems fair in a society which advocates as much egalitarianism as possible. Those who have higher incomes pay a higher percentage than those who earn less. However, Mr. Speaker, that is the role of government. They must establish a certain balance, see that a certain percentage of economic justice is applied to each individual and each taxpayer living in a country such as we know, Canada.
When he introduced his motion, the hon. member did not say that he wanted cuts in these areas. He did not talk about this. He did not say that there should be cuts in certain areas and increases in others so as to strike a certain balance. But experience tells us that when the income tax is reduced, the government must cut certain services, and too often, these cuts affect the social services. We have seen this in the past. Under the pretext that government spending must be cut, the governments have tended to reduce certain social services before introducing a balanced budget, even at the risk of causing
Taxation
some harship to those who are unable to contribute the equivalent because their income is lower than that of people in higher income brackets.
If this government could guarantee that this will not happen, if they could suggest a formula that would prove to me that they are able to go about it differently, I would certainly support their proposal because it would tend to increase indirectly the purchasing power of the disadvantaged without penalizing the efforts of the taxpayers with higher incomes because they work harder or have better positions.
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to talk about another point raised by the mover of the motion, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. Because of our taxation system, many of our Canadian brains go to the United States in search of less excessive taxation rates. Mr. Speaker, I must say that I am somewhat sceptic about this statement. What exactly is the brain drain? Have the people involved been identified? Has the public been told who are the people who flee to the United States because of inadequate incomes for the services they have rendered to the Canadian people? No mention is made of this. Mr. Speaker, who are those professionals rich enough to pay taxes here in Canada but who are so vain and materialistic that they move to a foreign country to increase their income? Very seldom low income earners because although they know they would pay fewer taxes in the United States they stay in Canada where they get more free social services than anywhere in the world.
However, Mr. Speaker, we should be realistic. Without advocating a socialistic system, through the years and following the representations from grass roots organizations to hon. members of various political parties, every one of us on various occasions has made representations to the government party which we usually call the party in power but which is not necessarily in power if the results achieved are any indication. Those results should be analysed on the basis of accounting revenues affecting the income of Canadians throughout the years, on the basis of the budgets proposed by the majority party, budgets which throughout the years increasingly affect the income of private citizens who have to pay for the social services demanded by the people, but for which the whole population has to pay. And I am upset when I hear in this House or on radio or TV a government member tell the people that if we have old age security in Canada we owe it to the Liberal party, that if we have family allowances we owe it to the Liberal party, and that if there is a guaranteed income supplement for people aged 60 or more living with a spouse aged 65 or more we owe it to the Liberal party. Mr. Speaker, I am upset by such assertions. After all, hon. members who have been sitting here for as many years as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and his colleagues of the same age have fought to push through parliament legislation recognizing the right to security and freedom in our country. We owe it to the work and efforts of these people throughout Canada who have done their best to develop our country and make it more affluent to ensure a certain security

May 23, 1978
Taxation
to senior citizens. But it is false to say that all that prosperity and our capacity to pay pensions to people aged 60, 65 or more is the result of the efforts made by the political party in power like the Liberal party. Because, Mr. Speaker, all Canadians whatever their age, whatever their political allegience have worked in agreement to give to our country this momentum toward prosperity so that it could give its aging citizens the possibility of enjoying this security, this assurance of going through their later days in a certain feeling of security coupled with a feeling of independence.
Mr. Speaker, today's young workers, and I have some among my relatives, as all members of this House probably have, these young people are working in conditions which are often difficult. Let us take for instance the case of construction workers. In summer time they have to withstand extremely difficult heat conditions which affects them considerably, and when winter comes, these same construction workers-and I am talking about them because I know their situation, Mr. Speaker, for if did not I would not speak so passionately about them-these same construction workers who are on the job, during December, January, February and March work through difficult conditions but they accept to do so and they also accept to pay on their wages a tax which will ensure the people who preceded them, their father, their uncle, relatives or just friends, some security for those who are over sixty because they recognize that while they are holding their jobs, they enjoy working conditions which are perhaps not always very advantageous but still better than those which prevailed some 40, 50, 60 years ago. These people accept to do their share to ensure their kind of security to the present generation of retired people.
Mr. Speaker, I understood the motion moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre to the effect that there is a difference between the conditions which prevail in the U.S. and in Canada. I also understand that there are Canadians working in lumber camps or elsewhere in the United States who pay taxes which are perhaps inferior to those which Canadians must pay when they work in Canada. Yet, Mr. Speaker, even if by that kind of work, even because of situations, conveniences, agreements which exist between the United States and Canada and even if there is a flight of Canadian capital to the United States which is detrimental to us, the fact remains, Mr. Speaker, that governments share a great responsibility in all that-

speechtext:
This debate is decidedly a non-event. After sitting here listening to what one of my old professors used to call pure and unmitigated eyewash or drivel, such as passed for a speech by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar, I feel perhaps I should counter some of the bold and bald assertions he made in that speech.
I do not propose to get into a lengthy debate on Canadian tax measures in comparison with United States tax measures. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) in a very able speech set out the main features of the Canadian tax system and the weaknesses, as we perceive them, of the United States tax system. On the facts the minister presented to us I am sure all members would agree there is no real comparison, and that in this country we do by and large have a very fair and equitable tax system.
I want to address my remarks to two particular points of view, the first of which deals with this comparative study of our lifestyle and standard of living with that of the United States. This does touch upon the general economic climate and tax systems of both countries. Secondly, I want to talk about one particular tax system, namely, sales tax as covered in the budget and which has been part of a national taxation or constitutional debate.
