speechtext:
An hon. member asks whether I am "going to muck that one up further". I think he should be patient, hear my remarks and then see how very ably I am going to try to expose the position of the Conservative party as being very duplicit, a position that most Canadians will see through on the election trail.
When we talk about comparisons between Canada and the United States the Conservative party is obsessed with the fact that everything south of the border is better than it is in this country. The minister said a number of times that the Conservative party is continually carping, complaining and tearing down our institutions and the confidence and morale of Canadians. This has some effect, and I do not deny that. When the official opposition in the House of Commons continues day after day to tear down the great confidence and feelings that we have developed in this country over the past 100 years, this does start to have some kind of effect on the Canadian people. I think many of our problems at this time result from lack of confidence, and that lack of confidence must be placed squarely at the doorstep of the official opposition.
When we talk about the United States let us consider a few basic facts. The per capita income in Canada is higher than it is in the United States, as supported by figures released recently, I think last week. This contradicts some of the suggestions of hon. members on the other side to the effect that this country is falling behind our American neighbours.
Taxation
Over the last ten years the disposable incomes of Canadians in Canada have been considerably higher than those in the United States. The number of new jobs that have been created in this country on a per capita or relative basis has been considerably greater not only than the number in the United States but also in all of the industrial trading nations in Europe and Japan, our major trading partners.
The official opposition will be riding in the next election, whenever that comes-this year, next year or whenever-on what I call the "Stirling Lyon white horse". It will be ridden across this country by those hon. members taking pot shots at our social services and at our bureaucracy. I do not think Canadians are going to buy their arguments, and those hon. members will find themselves in the same kind of difficulties their counterparts in Manitoba are finding themselves in now.
It is fine to talk about efficient and effective government. I think everyone on this side would agree that what we stand for is efficient and effective government. Over the last 30 years we have developed in this country, throughout all of industrialized society, a kind of social system, social tolerance and economy whereby a large number of people, perhaps the largest ever in history, have equitable access to income. I want to support that system as it has and is developed. I want to support the social programs which have been developed over the last 30 years. This does not mean to say we cannot administer those programs in a better way and thereby save taxpayers dollars.
Hon. members of the Conservative party, when comparing the United States and Canada, are always talking about our higher unemployment benefits. It is clear that the members who criticize our unemployment insurance system do not represent major urban constituencies. I do not hear very much criticism of UIC benefits from our Atlantic area colleagues. Those hon. members who criticize certainly do not represent constituencies in Quebec and northern Ontario where unemployment is high and where opportunities available in the relatively wealthy areas of southern Ontario and B.C. are not available to the people there.
I have to defend the unemployment insurance system we have today, and I am not embarrassed to do so. There have been some terrible administrative problems with that system, but those problems are being ironed out. It is true, perhaps, that some aspects of the system have encouraged disincentive to work, but simply to rip through this whole system, as some members opposite would do, solely in the guise of a work ethic, higher productivity and emulating the free enterprise of our American neighbours to the hilt, would be disastrous to many regions in this country.
Hon. members are very quick to criticize the universal and portable medicare system we have in this country, which the United States does not have. When they talk about the favourable position of the U.S. economic system, they fail to point out that many thousands of Americans every year are forced to pay hundreds if not thousands of dollars in medical coverage, which literally bankrupts whole families, causing a degree of hardship which I do not think any of us in this chamber would ever want to see return.

A federal-provincial conference was called and some good things came out of that, one of which was the sales tax proposal. It did not come from the federal government but from the government of Ontario. Members on the other side smirk about it, but this is the most fundamental and central issue facing this country at this time. The opposition does not want to talk about national unity, but here is an economic measure, this sales tax proposal, which is not only a taxation measure but something that affects the very fibre of the country. They cannot see that, however.
It has often been said that we are one of the most decentralized federations in the world. In the United States 60 per cent of all government revenues come under the control of Washington. It is the same in West Germany. But in this country it is only 40 per cent. The Bank of Canada is responsible to parliament through the Minister of Finance, yet 60 per cent of all government revenues is spent by municipal and provincial governments.
There is Bill Davis running off to Zurich and Rene Levesque running off to New York, borrowing money indiscriminately and not paying attention to how much interest has to be paid. What we need in this country is a centralized and economic planning system, and we are not getting it.

It pointed out about four main areas where the government has failed to tackle the economic needs of this country. I would like to read the motion that is before us today, as so many others have, because there are two important parts that I would like to refer to for a minute or two. The motion reads:
That a special committee of this House be established to determine whether the federal tax structure is inhibiting economic growth in Canada and promoting the export of employment opportunities to the United States.

On two consecutive days two opposition parties have each picked on this matter of the economy as being the key issue before us.
May 23, 1978

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-VALUE OF DOLLAR-EFFECT ON CANADIAN ENTREPRENEURS
THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-VALUE OF DOLLAR-EFFECT ON CANADIAN ENTREPRENEURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 5 I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) a question dealing with the value of the Canadian dollar, and in particular one aspect of it that has not been looked at. This concerns Canadian entrepreneurs selling in Canada having an advantage when the price of imports rises. The minister in his reply indicated that from March, 1977 to March, 1978 our exports increased from $40 billion to $50 billion. There was a 25 per cent increase in these exports which is certainly attributable to the change in the cost of the dollar. Also our imports did not increase over this period. In fact, we gained an advantage in this regard. Even though purchasing power did not increase during this period, it is obvious that Canadians were buying more Canadian goods.
A good many Canadians are concerned about the dollar. Perhaps there is more concern than is necessary. They are concerned that in some ways we are not as competitive as our neighbour to the south. Sometimes our costs of production have risen higher and faster than theirs. This is reflected in the value of the dollar.
There are other factors as well. There is the matter of pure speculation. That may have been ironed out to some extent at this point, given the fact that the dollar has been closer to 90 cents for the past few weeks. The government has taken some necessary steps to keep the swing from being too great. However, I would not like the government to do much more than it has done because there are some definite advantages to having an 89 or 90 cent dollar. One of the disadvantages has to do

May 23, 1978
Adjournment Debate
with inflation in terms of imported goods. With an 89 or 90 cent dollar, imported goods will cost ten or 11 cents more per dollar. That, of course, fuels inflation. If the dollar stabilized at this point, we would not expect a great deal more inflationary effect than that which has already occurred. There are two very definite advantages. One is well known to most Canadians, the advantage of being able to sell our exports in a more competitive way around the world.
The community from which I come and represent, part of Thunder Bay, is very fortunate. Last year it had one of the lowest rates of unemployment of any community in Canada with a population of over 100,000. A good deal of this can be attributed to the fact that our community does a geat deal of exporting.
Between 80 and 90 per cent of our pulp and paper is exported to the United States and other parts of the world. We are very heavily into the grain business with the largest grain port in Canada and one of the largest in the world. Exports in that area are supported by the lower dollar. This is one reason why there is a great advantage to having our dollar at around 90 cents in terms of American dollars.
The other advantage has not been discussed to any great extent. This is the whole point of my question. I refer to the advantage of Canadian entrepreneurs selling on the Canadian markets to Canadians and competing with imports from foreign countries.
When the cost of imports is higher, Canadian entrepreneurs have a great advantage in terms of competing with foreign goods. This area has not been looked at carefully enough by Canadian entrepreneurs. The federal government should be encouraging Canadian businesses to look at the higher cost of imports to see how we can compete in this market.
I would hope that if the dollar is held at 90 cents or 89 cents for a year or two a whole series of businesses will spring up able to compete with the higher cost imports, the greenhouse industry among a number of others would benefit a great deal from this situation. So I end by suggesting that the government should refrain from further support than what may be necessary to keep the dollar around 89 cents or 90 cents and that the dollar be allowed to float at that point in the hope that this will stimulate our export companies as well as many of our own industries which do business on the Canadian market.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ed Lumley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-VALUE OF DOLLAR-EFFECT ON CANADIAN ENTREPRENEURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. McRae) has stated, the recent decline in the external value of the dollar has improved the competitive position of Canadian firms by reducing the price of Canadian goods relative to foreign goods when measured in the same currency. The benefits to our exporters from this relative price change are clear. In fact in 1977, despite the relatively weak performance in the economies of most of our industrial trading partners, the volume of our merchandise exports increased by 10 per cent; preliminary indications for the first quarter of 1978
[Mr. McRae.)
suggest that this pace is being maintained. This is a direct benefit of the depreciation and has received fairly widespread recognition.
Hon. members are also aware that the other side of this coin is also important. Indeed, one of the main results of the rapid increase in Canadian costs and prices in the mid-70's was that Canadian producers were being squeezed out of our own market. The depreciation of the dollar has reversed this by raising the price Canadians must pay for imported goods, thus making home produced substitutes relatively cheaper. In quantitative terms, movements in the exchange rate since October 1976 have resulted in more than a 13 per cent increase in the relative price of goods imported from the United States.
The level of domestic demand stimulation induced by an exchange rate depreciation depends upon such factors as the availability of domestic substitutes and the ease with which Canadians can divert their expenditures towards domestically produced alternatives. In these terms, conditions in Canada have been favourable to take advantage of the exchange rate change.
The evidence amply demonstrates the impact of Canadian price performance on imports. Between 1973 and 1976 when the Canadian dollar was often above par with the U.S. dollar despite our unfavorable cost performance, merchandise imports rose over 13 per cent in volume at a time when g.n.p. grew only 10 per cent and exports declined. In 1977, however, imports rose only one per cent and by the end of the year were actually below year-earlier levels. The numbers so far available for the first quarter of 1978 suggest this favourable trend is continuing this year.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, the data support the view that the recent depreciation of the Canadian currency has aided Canadian business by improving its competitive position, not only abroad but also at home. As a result Canadian consumers are switching back from foreign produced imports to domestically produced goods to an important extent.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-BELL CANADA CONTRACT WITH SAUDI ARABIA
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-BELL CANADA CONTRACT WITH SAUDI ARABIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bell Canada has concluded an agreement to improve and operate the telephone system in Saudi Arabia from a contract worth more than $1 billion. Several hundred Canadian citizens will be working in that country. Bell Canada has assured Saudi Arabia under the agreement that it does not do business with the state of Israel. Prospective employees of Bell Canada who are to go to Saudi Arabia are required to fill out application forms which ask for their religion. There is evidence that Jewish applicants are not issued visas by Saudi Arabia.
When I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on May 5 whether he was aware of these discriminatory practices and whether he would take action to deal with this discriminatory situation, he evaded the issue, as he did on earlier occasions when answering similar questions by the hon. member for Windsor West (Mj. Gray). That Saudi policy, as I have
May 23, 1978

indicated, was proven in a recent United States court decision. The United States has passed two bills dealing with boycotts, such as the Arab boycott to which I have been referring. They are the tax reform act, 1976 and the export administration act, 1977. Under terms of those two bills U.S. companies are prohibited from signing contracts which contain boycott clauses of the kind Bell signed, or even from providing undertakings to the same effect.
The American system operates on the basis of the view that the Arab boycott is successful as long as uninvolved third parties, like U.S. or Canadian companies, agree to go along with boycott demands, as Bell Canada has done. The Americans argue, on the basis of a successful experience, that a refusal to go along with boycott demands does not lead to a loss of any trade. In fact, what happens is that it leads to renegotiation of contracts so that boycott undertakings are left out. United States laws are what give American companies their government's support in resisting these discriminating terms of trade.
Bell has admitted that its contract contains a so-called statement of fact that neither it, its associates or subsidiaries, have or are at present engaged in any business relationship with Israel. This clause is an intrinsic part of a five-year contract. This clause would, presumably, have to remain in place for the duration of the five-year contract. Bell spokesmen have admitted they have made a five-year undertaking with regard to this clause as well as the contract as a whole.
The Export Development Corporation has insured this contract for $430 million, the largest single insurance coverage in its history. Its president, John MacDonald, has said that this clause does not contravene the policy of the government because it is not overtly written in the future tense; that is, Bell does not agree that it will never deal with Israel in future. This distinction between present and future tense in a boycott undertaking, especially when the contract is clearly of a five-year duration, is a nonsensical distinction, yet it is distinctions of this kind which lie at the heart of the anti-boycott policy of the Canadian government and which, in my view, have made the Export Development Corporation a partner in this reprehensible contract.
I want to deal with the question of visas for Bell employees. It is the stated policy of Saudi Arabia not to grant visas or work permits to members of the Jewish faith. The only exceptions are officials of governments, important journalists, industrialists who accompany officials or those who have been individually approached by the Saudis and asked to come. All application forms for visas to Saudi Arabia contain requests for information, and at a further stage in the process proof in the form of a baptismal or other certificate regarding the religion of the application. All this is specifically requested for the purpose of selecting out and excluding Jews.
The United States government's policy on this issue, as given to American applicants for Saudi visas, is that the religion question should not be answered and that it should be
Adjournment Debate
left blank. The U.S. government has made representations to the Saudis which have succeeded in developing a situation in which Saudi visas are granted to U.S. citizens without any specification as to religion. It seems to me that Canada has the same moral obligation to its citizens and to its corporations as has the United States, and we could well take a leaf from the experience and the policies of the United States government.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Lapointe (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-BELL CANADA CONTRACT WITH SAUDI ARABIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have followed very closely the hon. member in his comments and there is something he did not mention, that we should congratulate ourselves that a Canadian corporation such as Bell Canada has their expertise recognized by a friendly country such as Saudi Arabia. It is all to our honour as Canadians that this corporation's technology is put to help a country technologically less developed than we are in building a large scale telephone network.
Turning to the substance of the question, namely the Arab boycott clause, I am not in a position to confirm whether Bell Canada signed that clause in their contract. I share the hon. member's concern that Canadians, and more specifically those to which we are addressing tonight, Canadians of Jewish origin, could be denied the right to work through Bell Canada in a country such as Saudi Arabia. However, I feel we must exercise a degree of caution, we should not suggest that certain things are done in the United States and we, in Canada, should sign a blank cheque or blindly follow what is now done in the United States. And it appears to me that I am not, nor is any member of this House in a position to state specifically that Bell Canada's contract with Saudi Arabia would have been refused under the American legislation.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that on various occasions the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) and the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicated our deep repulsion for any boycott clause, whether the anti-Jewish boycott as proposed by some Arabian countries, or any other boycott for that matter, and this country's reputation is by far the best among countries of the world in the matter of human rights. We have always made it a point, both in our domestic and foreign policies, to ensure equal status for all our citizens, equal rights to every citizen whatever his ethnic, national, racial or religious origin. I feel that Canada's record in that respect is one of the most glorious, and I have no fear whatever that the Canadian government will go on defending human rights, and certainly those of our own citizens.

subtopic: FISHERIES-ARRANGEMENTS WITH U.S. ON RECIPROCAL FISHING
FISHERIES-ARRANGEMENTS WITH U.S. ON RECIPROCAL FISHING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for some years now Canadian and U.S. fishermen have enjoyed reciprocity in fishing rights off Canadian and American waters. In 1976 and 1977 an agreement was signed between

May 23, 1978
Adjournment Debate
the two governments, but about three weeks ago some of the American fishermen decided to ask for a court injunction against Canadian fishermen fishing off the coast of the state of Washington. On May 3, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) spoke in Montreal, and one of the subtitles of his speech was "What can go wrong". On May 8 I rose in the House to ask the following question, with the preamble quoting the minister's statement:
As we know now on the west coast, plenty can go wrong. I would like to read a sentence or two from the joint report to the governments of Canada and the United States:
"The negotiators have agreed to recommend to governments the terms of interim arrangements to govern reciprocal fishing during 1978. The proposed arrangements would continue reciprocal fishing as previously agreed, with new mechanisms for consultation and resolution of differences and to help ensure that existing fishing patterns are maintained."
As I have said, previous to that joint statement the Americans had asked for a court injunction against Canadian fisheries. That is the backdrop to the problems we face today.
The proposed 1978 agreement also included expanding fishing areas in the U.S. waters for Canadian fishermen. So far as
I	know, to this day the United States Congress has not signed that agreement. I understand from a newspaper report of May
II	in Victoria that the American fishermen agreed to drop the court injunction because they fully believe that the Canadian fishermen will not get the expanded areas in the U.S. waters.
Since that time the Canadian authorities have agreed to close down the Swiftsure bank to Canadian and U.S. fishermen, even though the Canadian authorities see no threat to the salmon stock from fishing there. The U.S. authorities feel that it is a threat but, so far as I know, they will not share their information with Canadians. This means that Canadians have lost their fishing rights to the Swiftsure banks, they have lost the rights to American waters, and, as I say, the Americans have not allowed the Canadians into their waters, even though the Canadians have kept their part of the bargain, albeit perhaps a few days or a few weeks late.
According to the minister's answers to the questions from the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) a few days after I asked the question, the minister admitted that this might have been a bargaining position for the U.S. fishermen. It could well be that Canadians will never get the expanded fishing rights as proposed in the 1978 agreement. We are not talking about sport fishing or anything casual; we are talking about a major industry of Canada, and certainly of the Pacific coast. We are talking about a catch last year which amounted to 138 million pounds of salmon with a wholesale value of $230 million. The salmon resource base of British Columbia is the fourth most valuable primary industry. It supports 14,000 jobs, a large number of processing plants and a fleet of 5,000 vessels in the commercial industry.
I am concerned about the minister's answer to the question posed by the hon. member for New Westminster which reads as follows:

It is not as dramatic as the hon. member makes it sound. The fact is, however, that we have given the United States authorities a period of time in which to consult following the discussions which took place here last week. We have indicated that we cannot see a situation which would drag on all summer, because our fishermen would then be paying the price of the delay.
I might add that the significant fishery off the U.S. coast is not in early May but begins slightly later than that, and that our fishermen are still fishing off the coast of Alaska under the terms of the 1978 agreement.
How long is it going to be until we receive a firm commitment from the government that action against United States fishermen will be taken? Do our fishermen have to wait and wait until a decision is reached, during which time they lose their incomes? Do they have to sit by idly waiting for some casual agreement to take place before they can commence fishing? Are they to commence their fishing after the fish stock is gone, which has occurred in other years? Are they to sit by and let their livelihoods disappear while we take a casual approach to this matter?
